title: Salivary glands & saliva
blurb: The three pairs of major salivary glands, where their ducts open, what saliva contains and why a dry mouth is a dental problem.
question: A patient says that every time they start eating, a painful swelling comes up under their jaw and in the floor of the mouth, then slowly goes down after the meal. The dentist asks you to prepare for a lower occlusal radiograph. What is the likely cause, and which gland and duct are involved?

teach.body: Saliva comes from three pairs of major salivary glands (parotid, submandibular and sublingual) plus hundreds of tiny minor glands in the lips, cheeks, palate and tongue. Each major gland empties through a duct that opens at a set place in the mouth. Knowing those openings helps you understand swellings, blocked ducts and even where calculus builds up fastest.

teach.h: Duct openings and calculus hot spots
teach.caption: Calculus forms fastest near the duct openings: on the buccal surfaces of the upper molars (parotid) and the lingual surfaces of the lower incisors (submandibular and sublingual).

parotid: becomes the main source when you eat

teach.caption: Figures are approximate and vary between people. Most people make roughly half a litre to a litre and a half of saliva a day.

teach.body: Most salivary stones (calculi) form in the submandibular gland or Wharton's duct. The duct is long, runs upwards to the floor of the mouth, and its saliva is thicker and rich in calcium. When a stone blocks it, saliva can't escape. At mealtimes the gland is told to secrete, so it swells and hurts, then slowly settles. A lower occlusal radiograph can often show the stone in the floor of the mouth.

teach.h: Dry mouth (xerostomia) is a dental problem
teach.body: Without enough saliva, food and acid sit on the teeth for longer and nothing buffers or repairs them. Patients with a dry mouth get more caries (especially at the gum line and on roots), candida infection, trouble eating, speaking and wearing dentures, and altered taste. Common causes are medicines (such as some antidepressants, antihistamines and blood-pressure drugs), radiotherapy to the head and neck, Sjögren's syndrome, diabetes, dehydration and anxiety. The dentist may prescribe high-fluoride toothpaste and advise sips of water, saliva substitutes and sugar-free gum.

teach.text: Match the duct to the gland. STENSEN'S duct belongs to the PAROTID and opens on the cheek opposite the upper second molar (think S for Side of the cheek). WHARTON'S duct belongs to the SUBMANDIBULAR gland and opens under the tongue beside the lingual frenum (think W for Water under the tongue).

items: Parotid: largest, in front of the ear, watery saliva, Stensen's duct opposite the upper second molar.
Submandibular: most resting saliva, Wharton's duct beside the lingual frenum, most common site of stones.
Sublingual: smallest, under the tongue, thick mucous saliva, many small ducts.
Saliva lubricates, cleanses, buffers, remineralises, fights bacteria and starts starch digestion.
Swelling at mealtimes suggests a blocked duct; dry mouth raises caries risk.

summary: You can now name the three pairs of major salivary glands, say where each lies and where its duct opens, explain why a stone in Wharton's duct causes swelling at mealtimes, list what saliva contains and how each part protects the mouth, and explain why a dry mouth increases caries and other problems.

A.q: A patient has a swelling just in front of the ear that gets worse when they eat. Which gland is most likely affected?
options: A minor gland in the lip
A.why: The parotid gland lies in front of and below the ear and secretes heavily at mealtimes, so a blockage makes it swell then.

whyNot.0: The sublingual gland lies in the floor of the mouth under the tongue.
whyNot.1: The submandibular gland lies under the body of the mandible, not in front of the ear.
whyNot.3: Minor lip glands are tiny and would not cause swelling in front of the ear.

A.q: Where does the submandibular (Wharton's) duct open?
options: On the inner cheek opposite the upper second molar
On the palate behind the incisors
Floor of the mouth beside the lingual frenum
On the tip of the tongue
A.why: Wharton's duct opens on the sublingual papilla in the floor of the mouth, beside the lingual frenum.

whyNot.0: That is the opening of Stensen's (parotid) duct.
whyNot.1: No major salivary duct opens on the palate behind the incisors.
whyNot.3: No major duct opens on the tip of the tongue.

A.q: Which component of saliva helps neutralise acid after a sugary snack?
A.why: Bicarbonate is the main buffer in saliva, raising plaque pH back towards neutral after an acid attack.

whyNot.0: Amylase begins the digestion of starch.
whyNot.2: Mucin lubricates and helps form the pellicle.

B.q: Which gland produces most of the saliva in the mouth at rest, between meals?
B.why: The submandibular glands produce roughly 70% of resting (unstimulated) saliva.

whyNot.1: The parotid makes a smaller share at rest, but becomes the main source when eating.
whyNot.2: The sublingual glands contribute only a small amount.
whyNot.3: Minor glands add only a little to the total volume.

B.q: Heavy calculus keeps forming on the lingual surfaces of a patient's lower incisors. Why is this site so prone?
options: The tongue rubs plaque into it
It sits near salivary duct openings
The enamel there is much thinner
B.why: The submandibular and sublingual ducts open nearby, bathing these surfaces in mineral-rich saliva that calcifies plaque.

whyNot.0: The tongue does not cause calculus; mineral from saliva does.
whyNot.2: Enamel thickness does not determine where calculus forms.
whyNot.3: Fluoride reaches these surfaces; it is not related to calculus formation.

B.q: Which is NOT a usual cause of a dry mouth?
options: Radiotherapy to the head and neck
B.why: Sugar-free gum stimulates saliva flow; it is advised to relieve a dry mouth.

whyNot.0: Radiotherapy can permanently damage the salivary glands.
whyNot.1: Sjögren's syndrome is an autoimmune condition that attacks the salivary glands.
whyNot.2: Many medicines, including some antidepressants, reduce saliva flow.

C.q: During an examination, the dentist points to a small papilla on the inside of the cheek opposite the upper second molar. What opens there?
C.why: Stensen's duct carries saliva from the parotid gland and opens opposite the upper second molar.

whyNot.0: Wharton's duct opens in the floor of the mouth beside the lingual frenum.
whyNot.1: The sublingual ducts open along the floor of the mouth.
whyNot.3: The nasopalatine canal opens on the palate behind the upper incisors and carries a nerve, not saliva.

C.q: A swelling in the floor of the mouth worsens at mealtimes. In what order does saliva normally travel from the gland involved?
C.why: Saliva leaves the submandibular gland through Wharton's duct and enters the mouth beside the lingual frenum.

whyNot.0: Stensen's duct drains the parotid, which opens on the cheek, not the floor of the mouth.
whyNot.2: Saliva is made in the gland first, then carried by the duct.
whyNot.3: Saliva does not pass through lymph nodes.

C.q: Which salivary enzyme starts the digestion of starch?
C.why: Salivary amylase begins breaking starch down into sugars while food is still in the mouth.

whyNot.0: Pepsin digests protein in the stomach.
whyNot.1: Lipase digests fats, mainly in the small intestine.
whyNot.2: Lysozyme attacks bacterial cell walls; it doesn't digest starch.

reteach.title: Three taps, three pipes
reteach.question: Picture three pairs of taps feeding the mouth, each with its own pipe. Where does each pipe come out?

blocks.body: The biggest tap, the parotid, sits in front of your ear. Its pipe (Stensen's duct) runs across the cheek and comes out opposite your upper back teeth: run your tongue there and you may feel the little bump. The submandibular tap is under your jaw. Its pipe (Wharton's duct) runs forward under the tongue and opens either side of the little web of tissue that ties the tongue down (the lingual frenum). The smallest tap, the sublingual, sits right under the tongue and drips through lots of tiny pipes. If a pipe blocks, the tap still runs at mealtimes, so the gland swells.

rows.label: Opens
values: Floor of mouth, by lingual frenum

blocks.text: Swelling that comes up when eating and goes down afterwards is the classic sign of a blocked salivary duct.

explain.body: The largest gland, in front of and below the ear over the ramus. It makes watery saliva rich in amylase and is the main source when eating. Stensen's duct opens on the cheek opposite the upper second molar. The facial nerve runs through it.

test.q: Opposite which tooth does the parotid duct open?
test.why: Stensen's (parotid) duct opens on a small papilla in the cheek opposite the upper second molar.

whyNot.0: No major duct opens opposite the lower first molar.
whyNot.2: The parotid duct opens further back than the canine.
whyNot.3: The ducts near the lower incisors are the submandibular and sublingual.

explain.body: Under the body of the mandible. It produces most resting saliva. Wharton's duct runs forward and upwards to open beside the lingual frenum. Its long, uphill duct and thicker saliva make it the commonest site for stones.

test.q: Why are salivary stones most common in the submandibular gland and duct?
options: Its duct is short and straight
It has no duct at all
test.why: Wharton's duct is long and runs upwards, and its saliva is thicker and calcium-rich, so stones form more easily.

whyNot.0: The duct is long, not short.
whyNot.1: Its saliva is mixed and thicker than the parotid's.

explain.body: The smallest major gland, lying in the floor of the mouth under the tongue. It makes thick, mainly mucous saliva and empties through many small ducts along the floor of the mouth.

test.q: Which gland is the smallest of the major salivary glands?
test.why: The sublingual gland, under the tongue, is the smallest of the three pairs.

whyNot.2: The submandibular is mid-sized and makes most resting saliva.
whyNot.3: The lacrimal gland makes tears, not saliva.

explain.body: It lubricates, cleanses, buffers acid (bicarbonate), remineralises enamel (calcium, phosphate, fluoride), controls bacteria (lysozyme, IgA), starts starch digestion (amylase) and helps taste and swallowing. Lose it and caries risk rises.

test.q: A patient on several medicines has a very dry mouth. Which problem are they most at risk of?
test.why: Less saliva means less buffering, cleansing and remineralisation, so caries risk rises, especially at the gum line and on roots.

whyNot.0: Calculus forms from mineral in saliva, so less saliva doesn't increase it.
whyNot.1: Gingival overgrowth is linked to specific drugs, not dry mouth itself.
whyNot.2: Eruption timing in adults is not affected by dry mouth.
